newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico to restrict pension fund investments in '97.
newsitem.headline: Mexico to restrict pension fund investments in '97.

text.p: Preliminary rules drawn up for Mexico's emerging private pension system limit investments in its first year to safe, mostly inflation-indexed securities, a senior official said.

Daniel Lederman, vice president of planning at the pension regulatory commission Consar, told Reuters late Thursday that fund management firms, known as Afores, would only be able to offer one choice of pension fund to clients in their first year to ensure there are no potentially scandalous losses.

"It is predicted that at the beginning there will only be one investment fund. Most of the investment instruments (in it) will have to be indexed, like UDIs, though not all," he said. UDIs are inflation-index Units of Investment that guarantee real returns.
"After the first year, the client can ask to diversify."

The rules governing the Afores, which are due to start operating on Jan. 1, 1997, have still to be signed into law by President Ernesto Zedillo. Lederman said he expected they would see the president's pen within the next few weeks.

Given that Mexicans have never had the option to pick from a choice of pension funds with differing returns, he said it was important they not be confused by too many investment options in the first year.
After a tough wrangle to win political acceptance for ending the current state-run scheme, he also noted the importance of avoiding steep losses at the outset.
"It was a difficult change from a political point of view and we have to be careful there are (positive) returns."
Critics say a decision to restrict investments in the first year to such low-risk, low-return investments as UDIs may damage the credibility of the scheme.
"It's a total controversy," said Ernesto O' Farrill, head of Bursametrica, an economic consulting firm that has been working closely with Afores as they start setting up.
"If you limit the investment regime to UDIs you're going to hurt the system...there will be little competitiveness and you won't be able to see which are the best Afores."
But Lederman stressed the funds would not be strictly restricted to UDIs. Some other securities would be allowed.

The Consar official also sought to soothe fears that the system would not be ready in time for start-up in January, though he acknowledged there had been delays in drawing up regulations to govern the industry.

The delays, he said, have been caused by the complexity of the system, trying to reach a consensus among all the government agencies and financial firms involved. He did not rule out some hold up, however.
"It should be ready in January," he said. "Until we see when the regulations are published we can't be sure."
